input:
Case

This proposal sets out the case for fitting a solar installation on the roof of the building, and seeks approval to proceed to the stage of detailed design. The building currently purchases the whole of its electricity, and generation on the roof would act to displace purchased electricity during those hours when the building is occupied and the array is generating. The roof represents, in effect, the one surface available on the site which is capable of accommodating an array without encroaching upon land, yard space, or parking, and it is at present entirely unused. The case for the installation rests substantially upon the match which exists between generation and use: the building is occupied throughout the daylight hours, with the welcome consequence that the greater part of the generation is consumed on site at the very moment it is produced, and only the surplus arising at weekends and during the brightest periods is exported. Since export is worth appreciably less than displaced purchase, the value of the installation stands or falls on self-consumption, and the case has accordingly been stated on that basis. It is to be noted that the case presupposes no change in the building's use or in the level of its demand: the array is sized against the demand which the building already exhibits, and any fall in demand would diminish both the self-consumed share and the value along with it. Detailed design constitutes the stage at which the output of the actual roof is properly established, by reference to its orientation, its shading, and the area which the structure permits to be covered, rather than by reference to the generic figures which a case at the present stage is obliged to employ.

Costs

The capital cost of the installation is $1334k. The appraisal has been carried out over a horizon of 15 years, and the costs and savings falling within that horizon are those of the installation itself: the maintenance of the array and of its mountings, cleaning in so far as the exposure of the roof renders cleaning necessary, insurance, and the replacement of the inverters, which falls inside the horizon and is treated as a cost of the project rather than as a cost of the building. Set against these costs are the savings: the purchased electricity displaced by generation consumed on site, valued at the tariff which the building pays, together with the more modest return obtained on exported surplus. The capital cost of $1334k is to be understood as a budget figure at this stage; it will be fixed by tender following detailed design, and the appraisal will be rerun on the tendered figure before any decision regarding construction is taken. The savings appearing in the appraisal are estimates derived from the expected output of the roof and from the tariff currently in force; no output has as yet been measured on the building, and the appraisal accordingly records the savings as estimates throughout. The sensitivity of the case is, in essence, the sensitivity of these two figures: a tender exceeding the budget figure and an output falling short of the estimate act upon the return in one and the same direction, and either of them alone suffices to narrow the margin which the case presents. For the avoidance of doubt, the capital figure embraces the design, the surveys, the array together with its mountings, the inverters, the connection, and the metering; it does not embrace renewal of the roof covering itself, which forms part of the building's own programme and would fall to be spent whether the installation proceeded or not, so that to charge it to the project would be to charge one and the same item of work to two budgets simultaneously. The savings, for their part, are valued year by year at the tariff in force at the date of the appraisal, held level throughout the horizon; a rise in the tariff would enhance the value of the purchase displaced and would thereby improve the return, whilst a fall would act in precisely the contrary direction, and the appraisal, it should be noted, takes credit for neither movement, the return being presented throughout at present prices.

Schedule

Work will commence one quarter after approval has been given. The first stage consists of the detailed design itself, with the structural survey of the roof and the application for the connection being progressed within it. Procurement follows on from the design: the array, the mountings, and the inverters will be ordered once the design has fixed their respective specifications, and it is the lead times attaching to those orders which determine the interval which must elapse before installation can begin. Installation is to be planned in such a manner as to keep the building in use throughout, the roof work being sequenced so that the building remains weather-tight at the conclusion of each stage of the mounting work, and the electrical connection being effected in a single planned interruption arranged in agreement with the occupants. Commissioning brings the sequence to a close: the generation meter is fitted, the export arrangement is registered, and the output is read against the estimate from the first period of operation onwards. No contractor is named in this proposal; appointment will follow the tender which the detailed design serves to prepare, and the schedule has accordingly been stated in terms of stages reckoned from approval rather than in terms of dates drawn from a contractor's programme.

Decision requested

The decision which is requested is approval to proceed to detailed design, and not to construction. Detailed design will settle the questions which the case, at this stage, cannot: whether the structure of the roof is capable of carrying the array and its mountings with the margin which the structure requires, what layout is left available by the roof's obstructions and shading, what the connection will cost and on what terms the export will be accepted, and what fixed price the tender will return. Each of these answers bears directly upon the figures which the appraisal presents. Construction represents a second and separate decision, to be taken when the design and the tender price are both in hand, and this proposal seeks no commitment whatsoever to it at the present time. Approval of detailed design commits the design fee and the costs of the surveys, and nothing beyond them. Should the design demonstrate that the roof cannot carry the array, or should the tender return a price at which the appraisal fails, the project comes to a halt at that point, with the design costs expended and the construction cost remaining uncommitted. The board is therefore asked to approve the design stage, on the basis of the appraisal as stated, with the decision on construction expressly reserved. The alternatives open to the board at this juncture are three in number: to approve the design stage, to defer a decision, or to decline the installation altogether. Deferral preserves every option and involves the expenditure of nothing, albeit at the cost of separating the installation from the roof works and of reopening the appraisal in due course at the prices of a later date. Declining brings the matter to a definitive close and leaves the building dependent, as at present, upon purchased electricity in its entirety. Approval, by contrast, is the sole alternative which generates the evidence — the survey report upon the structure, the layout which the roof proves capable of accepting, the offer of connection together with its terms, and the price returned by tender — upon which a properly informed decision as to construction can subsequently be founded, and it is accordingly the course which this proposal commends to the board.

Progress through the design stage is reported to the board at its regular meetings, against the stages stated here, and any slip in the connection step is reported at the meeting after it is known, since the connection date is the date the installation sequence hangs from.

The decision requested is approval to proceed to detailed design, not to construction. Detailed design settles the questions the case cannot: whether the roof structure carries the array and its mountings with the margin the structure requires, what layout the roof's obstructions and shading leave available, what the connection costs and on what terms the export is taken, and what fixed price the tender returns.
